answer_en: Answer: The popular initiative "For a better life in old age (initiative for a 13th AHV pension)" would have different effects on old-age pensioners compared to recipients of IV pensions or survivors' pensions. While old-age pensioners would receive an annual supplement equivalent to one-twelfth of their annual pension, recipients of IV pensions or survivors' pensions would not receive such a supplement. This would lead to unequal treatment between the different groups of pension recipients (p. 9).

Answer: According to the dispatch, the revenue deficit of the AHV would amount to around 8.7 billion francs in 2032 (p. 10). The expenditures of the AHV would be increased by around 5 billion francs, and the federal share of the additional expenditures would amount to around 1 billion francs (p. 10).

The initiative committee justifies the necessity of a supplement to the OASI old-age pensions by stating that the current amount of the OASI old-age pensions is too small for low to medium income classes to guarantee adequate financial security for pensioners when transitioning into retirement. They argue that half of all individuals who retired in 2018 had to make do with less than CHF 1,772 in OASI pension per month and that many individuals, especially women, were unable to supplement this income or could only do so to a limited extent through their pension fund. Furthermore, almost every tenth person was directly dependent on supplementary benefits after retirement. The initiative committee is of the opinion that a supplement to the OASI old-age pension is necessary to secure the existence of pensioners, especially for those with low wages during their gainful employment. They also emphasize that the decreasing replacement rate of the OASI and the mechanism of the pension index further increase the need for a supplement (p. 4-5).

The dispatch considers the effects of the initiative on generational justice to be problematic. It argues that today's and future gainfully employed individuals already have to bear a high burden in order to secure the previous level of benefits, and that these burdens are higher than those which the majority of today's pensioners had to bear during their gainful employment. The dispatch therefore questions whether it is justified to grant current old-age pensioners an additional supplement which they do not finance or only finance to a small extent (p. 18).

According to the dispatch, the Federal Council predicts additional expenditure of around 5 billion francs for the old-age and survivors' insurance (AHV) in the year 2032 if the popular initiative "Für ein besseres Leben im Alter (Initiative für eine 13. AHV-Rente)" is accepted (p. 10).
The initiators propose that, in addition to the increase of wage percentages, a part of the profits of the National Bank be used for financing the supplement (p. 12).
Answer: According to the dispatch, 101,793 valid signatures were collected for the popular initiative "For a better life in old age (initiative for a 13th AHV pension)" (p. 3).
According to the dispatch, this proportion is 26 percent.

Answer: The Federal Council wants to reject the initiative for a 13th AHV pension because it is of the opinion that the financial challenges of the AHV are already great and would be exacerbated by the adoption of the initiative. The additional expenditure of around 5 billion francs in 2032 would increase the pay-as-you-go deficit of the AHV and enlarge the financing gap. Furthermore, the Federal Council is of the opinion that the initiative is not effective because it does not make any differentiation between pension recipients and thus would also favour better-off pensioners. The Federal Council prefers a comprehensive reform of old-age provision, such as the planned reform AHV 21, which is intended to secure the level of benefits and financing of the AHV in the long term (p. 2-5, p. 10-12).

The Federal Council wants to reject the initiative for a 13th AHV pension because it creates unequal treatment within the 1st pillar, as only old-age pensioners and not also disability or survivor's pensioners are privileged. This contradicts the constitutional purpose of the pensions of the 1st pillar, which are intended to adequately cover the need for existence. Furthermore, the initiative would exacerbate the financial challenges of the AHV and lead to an increased burden on contributors. The Federal Council prefers a comprehensive reform of old-age provision that ensures the level of benefits and financing of the AHV and occupational pension provision, rather than one-sided measures like the initiative for a 13th AHV pension (p. 10).

According to the dispatch, the annual expenditure of the old-age and survivors' insurance (AHV) would increase by around 5 billion francs if the initiative "For a better life in old age (initiative for a 13th AHV pension)" is accepted.

The financing of these additional expenditures is not specified in the initiative. However, various possibilities are being discussed, such as increasing payroll contributions or using parts of the profits of the National Bank. Nevertheless, using National Bank profits without a constitutional amendment would burden the Confederation and thus not represent a genuine financing solution.

It is also mentioned that the initiative would lead to an increased burden on the federal budget, since the Confederation already covers 20.2% of AHV expenditures today. To finance these additional expenditures, either other expenditures would have to be reduced or new sources of revenue would have to be tapped. One possible option could be an increase in value-added tax, which would also require a constitutional amendment. (p. 10-15)

Answer: The 13th AHV pension would increase the proportion of the AHV old-age pension in total income for persons with low pension fund benefits, who tend to be more dependent on the AHV (p. 16). In contrast, such a supplement would be hardly or not at all socially justified for retirees from higher income classes (p. 2).

Answer: A cancellation of the FZA would, due to the guillotine clause (Art. 25 para. 4 FZA), lead to the elimination of the Bilateral I agreements. Through the guillotine clause, six months after notification, all agreements of the Bilateral I affected by this clause automatically cease to apply. Thus, with the FZA, the agreements on public procurement, the reduction of technical trade barriers, trade in agricultural products, and land and air transport would also become obsolete. (p. 66)

Answer: The Federal Council assumes that the elimination of the Schengen and Dublin association agreements would mean negative effects on economic development and additional costs. By 2030, the gross domestic product could be 1.6–3.7 percent lower according to estimates from 2018. Per capita income could decrease by 700–1600 francs depending on the scenario. The border regions and the tourism sector would be particularly affected by the elimination of facilitations in travel traffic and by systematic border controls (p. 67).

Answer: The Federal Council is aware that immigration and the associated population growth pose challenges. Numerous strategies and measures are already in place or being developed to address these challenges in various areas. On 29 January 2025, the Federal Council defined further measures in the area of asylum, immigration into the labour market, and housing to reduce immigration and address the challenges of immigration. These accompanying measures are not conceived as a direct counter-proposal or indirect counter-suggestion to the initiative. The Federal Council considers these strategies and measures to be more effective in addressing the challenges posed than the adoption of the popular initiative "No 10-million Switzerland!". It therefore rejects the initiative and recommends that the federal chambers submit it to the people and cantons for a vote without a direct counter-proposal or indirect counter-suggestion, with the recommendation to reject the popular initiative.

Answer: The Federal Council rejects the initiative because it considers it unrealistic and fears that its implementation would lead to a cancellation of the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons (AFMP) with the EU. This would have severe financial, economic, and social consequences for Switzerland and could also lead to the cancellation of further bilateral agreements with the EU. The Federal Council prefers instead a stabilization and further development of the bilateral path with the EU and wants to adhere to the proven migration policy and humanitarian principles. It is aware of the challenges posed by immigration and has defined additional measures to take into account population development (p. 82).

The immigration to Switzerland over the last decades was strongly influenced by economic development. The favourable economic development after the Second World War triggered a strong demand for foreign workers in Switzerland. This could not be fully covered by the domestic population. Therefore, workers were mainly recruited from Italy. They found employment particularly in seasonal industries such as agriculture and construction, as well as in industry. Despite the economic recession in the mid-1970s and cantonal quotas for annual residents and seasonal workers, which followed the so-called rotation principle from the mid-1960s, the foreign population continued to grow over the years. Between 1960 and 1974, an average of 108,000 employed foreigners and an additional 205,000 seasonal workers immigrated to Switzerland's permanent resident population each year. In the following decades, Switzerland recorded lower immigration figures. Between 1975 and 2001, the immigration of employed foreigners (permanent resident population) was 37,900 people and 110,000 seasonal workers per year. While the immigration of employed persons experienced a temporary upswing in the 1980s due to the favourable economic situation, it declined significantly in the 1990s against the backdrop of the major economic crisis. In 2002, the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons (FZA) with the EU came into force and enabled free movement between Switzerland and the EU/EFTA states. The immigration of workers from EU/EFTA states, both in terms of scope and occupational or qualification-specific composition, is determined and controlled by the development of labour demand by companies in Switzerland. In contrast, the immigration of non-employed persons was low. The increase in employment over the past two decades was particularly strong in the area of demanding, education-intensive activities. Many of the EU workers currently employed in Switzerland are employed in these strongly growing economic sectors, such as in the field of freelance, scientific and technical services, the information and communication sector, or in the health care system. These highly qualified foreign workers made a significant contribution to the fact that the Swiss economy was able to successfully specialize in knowledge-intensive value creation over the past few years and thus strengthen its resilience and positioning in international competition. However, Switzerland also relies on immigrants from the EU area when recruiting workers for simpler tasks in the hospitality industry, construction, and industry, as these positions can no longer be fully filled domestically, among other things due to the higher qualification of the domestic population. In the face of advancing demographic ageing, the recruitment of foreign workers to cover labour demand will gain additional importance in the coming years. According to the Federal Statistical Office (BFS) scenarios on demographic development, future growth of the working-age population will depend even more strongly on immigration than before. At the same time, the scope for better exploiting the domestic labour potential is limited; the employment rate of the native population is very high today and unemployment is persistently low - results that also suggest that immigration has not affected the employment opportunities of native workers. Against this background, it can be assumed that a repeal of the FZA and the introduction of a more administered immigration regime with quantitative limits on immigration would significantly reduce the growth potential of the Swiss economy and further accentuate the challenges associated with demographic change.

Answer: According to the dispatch, a termination of the FZA due to the guillotine clause (Art. 25 para. 4 FZA) would lead to the elimination of the Bilateral I agreements, which would also render the agreements on public procurement, the reduction of technical trade barriers, trade in agricultural products, and land and air transport ineffective. Furthermore, there is a possibility and thus a risk that the EU will also call into question other agreements with Switzerland that it considers to be connected to the FZA, particularly the SAA and the DAA. A termination of the FZA could also jeopardize the EFTA Agreement, as this is based on the bilateral treaties between Switzerland and the EU.

Answer: The initiative demands that the permanent resident population of Switzerland be limited to under ten million by the year 2050. From 2050, the Federal Council can increase the limit annually by ordinance by the surplus of births (p. 37).

Answer: The popular initiative "Keine 10-Millionen-Schweiz! (Nachhaltigkeitsinitiative)" [No 10-million Switzerland! (Sustainability Initiative)] provides that the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons (AFMP) with the EU must be terminated if the permanent resident population of Switzerland exceeds the ten million threshold for two years and no exception or safeguard clauses have been negotiated or invoked by then, with which compliance with the ten million threshold can be achieved (p. 63).

Answer: The Federal Council argues that the cancellation of the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons (AFMP) with the EU and the introduction of a restrictive immigration mechanism would have significant financial, economic, and social consequences. It emphasizes that the Swiss economy is dependent on foreign workers, particularly in the area of demanding, education-intensive activities. The immigration of highly qualified EU workers has significantly contributed to knowledge-intensive value creation and to strengthening resilience and positioning in international competition. The Federal Council is aware that immigration poses challenges, but it considers the existing strategies and measures to be effective in addressing the challenges posed (p. 64).

Answer: If Switzerland has more than ten million inhabitants, it must cancel the agreement on the free movement of persons with the EU according to the initiative. This would have significant effects on the economy, as the agreement regulates important economic relations between Switzerland and the EU. The cancellation would lead to a lapse of the FZA, which in turn would call into question the bilateral path with the EU. This would have negative effects on economic development, as Switzerland benefits from close relations with the EU and these are important for its economic development. The lapse of the FZA would also lead to a loss of legal certainty and a reduction in location attractiveness. Furthermore, it would be difficult for Switzerland to recover from the negative effects of a cancellation of the agreement, as this would lead to a deterioration of the economic framework conditions and a reduction in competitiveness. (p. 66)

Answer: The limitation of the population number to ten million could possibly contribute to alleviating the housing shortage. The Federal Council has already proposed an action plan against the housing shortage that contains over 30 measures. In addition, it plans to increase the fund for promoting non-profit housing construction by a total of 150 million francs in order to create more affordable apartments. Furthermore, the conditions for foreign nationals who want to acquire land in Switzerland or rights thereto are to be tightened.

Answer: The dispatch emphasizes that the current neutrality practice is flexible and enables Switzerland to adapt its neutrality to changed circumstances. In contrast, the neutrality initiative would anchor a rigid understanding of neutrality in the Federal Constitution, which would restrict flexibility in the application of neutrality. The dispatch argues that this restriction of flexibility could have negative effects on the security, economic, and foreign policy of Switzerland (p. 2-3, p. 21-23).

Answer: According to the dispatch, the good offices play an important role as an element of Swiss foreign policy. Neutrality can contribute to the credibility of this commitment. The initiative states that Switzerland should use its permanent neutrality for the prevention and resolution of conflicts and make itself available as a mediator (Art. 54a para. 4 E-BV). However, the explicit enshrinement of this goal has no implications for neutrality policy, since good offices are also possible without neutrality and political weight, multilateral competences, discretion, and experience with cultural diversity are important factors for this (p. 22).

Answer: The dispatch states that the neutrality initiative would restrict Switzerland's sanctions policy. While Switzerland currently supports internationally broadly supported sanctions, the initiative would call this into question. The adoption of sanctions by the OSCE, the EU or other important trading partners against warring states would be excluded. This could lead to reputational damage and foreign, security and economic policy consequences (p. 25).

Answer: The Federal Council recommends the rejection of the initiative because it would lead to a clear change of course in Swiss neutrality, which would have negative effects on Switzerland's security, economic and foreign policy. The initiative would restrict flexibility in the application of neutrality and hinder Switzerland's ability to respond to new challenges. Furthermore, the initiative would make security policy cooperation with other states and organisations more difficult and weaken Switzerland's defence capability (p. 2-3).

According to the dispatch, neutrality is not explicitly defined in the Swiss Federal Constitution (BV), but rather results from international law. The BV establishes neutrality in the competency order of the federal authorities and provides that the Federal Council and the Federal Assembly shall take "measures for the preservation [...] of the neutrality of Switzerland" (Art. 173 para. 1 lit. a and 185 para. 1 BV). Several federal laws refer to neutrality explicitly or implicitly without, however, defining it in terms of content. The first official declaration of neutrality was proclaimed by the Old Confederacy at the Tagsatzung of 1674 and the European great powers recognized the perpetual neutrality of Switzerland for the first time under international law at the Paris Peace Conference in 1815.
The Federal Chancellery established by decree of 28 May 2024 that the initiative had been successful with 129,806 valid signatures (p. 4).

The Federal Council stated upon Switzerland's accession to the UN in 2002 that Switzerland retains its neutrality and thereby confirmed its parallel obligations under neutrality law and the UN Charter.

Answer: According to the initiative text, Switzerland is only allowed to cooperate with military or defence alliances if it concerns the case of a direct military attack on Switzerland or actions preparing such an attack (p. 16).

The initiative would, according to the Federal Council, lead to a significant restriction of the security policy cooperation of Switzerland with military and defence alliances. This would result in a weakening of the defensive capability of Switzerland, as Switzerland benefits from the cooperation with these alliances and they are important for maintaining its security. The initiative would also make it more difficult for Switzerland to participate in international cooperation projects that are important for security and defence, such as the exchange of information on threats or the training of specialist personnel. This could impair Switzerland's ability to respond to security-related challenges. (p. 24)

Answer: The Federal Council wants to reject the neutrality initiative because anchoring a specific understanding of neutrality in the federal constitution would lead to a departure from flexible practice. Swiss neutrality was never rigid and an end in itself, but has resulted from the contemporary context since its beginnings and oriented itself according to the respective international realities and Swiss interests in foreign and domestic policy. The initiative would anchor neutrality as a principle of foreign policy, which would reduce the scope for flexible use of neutrality. This would not be in the interest of Switzerland, as flexibility in handling neutrality within the framework of applicable international law is of central importance for the optimal safeguarding of Swiss national interests (p. 14).

Answer: The initiative wants to preserve Swiss neutrality and provides that Switzerland should use its permanent neutrality for the prevention and resolution of conflicts and be available as a mediator (Art. 54a para. 4 E-BV). However, the rigid anchoring of a specific understanding of neutrality in the Federal Constitution could restrict the flexibility of Switzerland in applying neutrality and make it more difficult to respond to changed circumstances. This could lead to the fact that Switzerland can no longer effectively fulfill its role as a mediator (p. 14). Furthermore, the initiative could restrict the security and defense policy cooperation of Switzerland with other states, which in turn could impair the ability of Switzerland to act as a mediator (p. 24). It is therefore questionable whether the initiative actually strengthens neutrality or rather weakens it.

Answer: No, according to the initiative text, Switzerland may not impose non-military coercive measures (sanctions) on warring states, except in the area of the UN. The initiative refers here to the international law obligation of Switzerland to implement the sanctions enacted by the UN Security Council. (p. 18)

Answer: The initiative provides that Switzerland is to use its neutrality for the prevention and resolution of conflicts and is to be available as a mediator. This means that Switzerland wants to strengthen its role as a mediator in conflicts in order to promote peaceful solutions. However, the rigid anchoring of neutrality in the constitution could also lead to Switzerland being less flexible when it comes to responding to changed circumstances and adapting its role as a mediator. (p. 14)

The popular initiative "For a civil status-independent individual taxation (Tax Justice Initiative)" pursues the goal of achieving civil status-independent taxation of natural persons. This means that all persons are to be taxed individually, regardless of their civil status.

The Federal Council's indirect counter-proposal has similar goals: It is intended to introduce individual taxation and thus achieve neutral taxation with regard to civil status. The Federal Council proposes that married couples should be taxed individually, just like unmarried couples, in order to abolish the so-called "marriage penalty" and increase the employment incentives for second earners. The Federal Council wants to promote equal rights for women and men and improve equal opportunities on the labour market.

Both proposals aim to improve tax justice and take into account the economic performance of individuals. They are intended to contribute to ensuring that all persons are taxed fairly and justly, regardless of their civil status.

Answer: Under the current law, married couples are taxed jointly, with their incomes added together and taxed according to a special tariff. In contrast, under the proposed individual taxation, each spouse is taxed individually, regardless of marital status, and taxpayers are taxed according to a uniform tariff. The income and assets are assigned to the spouses according to civil law relationships or other statutory entitlements.

Answer: The individual taxation leads to a reduction of the tax burden on the second income for married couples, which increases the employment incentives for secondary earners. In contrast to today's joint taxation, where the couple is taxed as an economic community and the second income is taxed based on the first income, individual taxation results in reduced tax burden for secondary earners. This can particularly affect women, who in most cases achieve the second income in married couples. The more even distribution of gainful employment strengthens the financial independence of both spouses and leads to better provision for old age and in view of a possible divorce. This is also in line with the more recent federal court case law on post-marital maintenance, which gives greater weight to the principle of self-sufficiency after divorce.

The Federal Council rejects the initiative and opposes it with the federal act on individual taxation as an indirect counter-proposal. The reasons for this are:
- The elimination of the marriage penalty in direct federal tax has been pending for around 40 years.
- With an anchoring of civil status-independent taxation at constitutional level, there would be a binding decision on direction for the legislator, but measures to implement the new constitutional provision would still be necessary.
- The introduction of individual taxation is also possible without a provision at constitutional level. In terms of time, the way via legislation leads faster to the goal.
- The anchoring of the taxation method (jointly for [married] couples or individually) in the constitution restricts the legislator.
- A corresponding bill was already being drafted, as the parliament commissioned the Federal Council in the legislative planning 2019–2023 to submit a proposal to it for the introduction of individual taxation.

The estimated reduced revenues from direct federal tax due to the introduction of individual taxation amount to around 1 billion francs in the tax year 2024. Of this, approximately 800 million francs affect the Confederation and approximately 200 million francs affect the cantons (p. 12).

According to the dispatch (p. 4), the number of additional tax returns that must be processed nationwide due to the introduction of individual taxation is approximately 1.7 million. This corresponds to an increase of around one third.

The introduction of individual taxation leads to an adjustment of the tariff codes for withholding tax. The existing tariff codes for married one- and two-income earners as well as for single people with children are adjusted or deleted. New tariff codes must be created for German and Italian cross-border commuters. The adjustment of the tariff codes is intended to simplify withholding tax, for example by eliminating the distinction between one- and two-income earners.

Answer: In the case of married couples with a 90/10 income distribution without children, additional burdens arise from a total income of the married couple of around 30,000 francs. The tariff adjustment reduces the additional burden, particularly in the low and medium incomes, but cannot fully compensate for it. (p. 83)

Answer: The Federal Council wants to abolish the marriage penalty with individual taxation because this can lead to a better exploitation of the domestic labour and skilled workforce potential. The loss of tax revenue of one billion francs is a price that the Federal Council is willing to pay for increasing the employment incentives for second earners. The Federal Council assumes that individual taxation will primarily encourage women to take up gainful employment or increase their workload, which in turn can lead to better economic security for many women and a strengthening of the financial independence of both spouses. This is also in line with the more recent federal court case law on post-marital maintenance, which gives greater weight to the principle of self-sufficiency after divorce. The Federal Council is of the opinion that it is constitutionally justifiable if no corrective measure is provided for one-income couples and two-income couples with low second income (p. 18).

Answer: The Federal Council can describe individual taxation as beneficial for the equality of women and men because it leads to women in marriages becoming financially more independent and being able to take up or expand their own gainful employment. This in turn strengthens their position in their profession and in society and promotes the equality of women and men. Individual taxation also leads to the tax burden no longer being shifted to the joint income of the couple, but rather to the individual income of each person. This can contribute to women, who often have lower incomes than their male partners, no longer being disadvantaged and being able to improve their own financial situation. (p. 104)

The individual taxation leads to the fact that the tax system hinders the taking up or expansion of a second income less. This should lead to a higher labour force participation of secondary earners. In particular, women, who in most cases achieve the second income in married couples, will benefit from this. The more even distribution of gainful employment strengthens the financial independence of both spouses and leads, especially for many women, to better provision for old age and with regard to a possible divorce. This is also in line with the more recent federal court case law on post-marital maintenance, which gives greater weight to the principle of self-support after divorce. (p. 103)

In the case of married couples living separately, the tax assessment is not directly influenced by the fact of living apart. The tax assessment is carried out according to the same rules as for married couples living together, i.e. they are taxed jointly and must submit a joint tax return. However, the fact of living apart can have effects on the tax situation, particularly when it comes to the division of income, assets or deductions. In such cases, the tax assessment can become more complicated since the spouses manage their financial affairs separately and the tax implications are affected by this. It is however important to note that the tax laws and regulations in this area are very specific and can vary from case to case. It is advisable to consult a tax expert or tax consultant to ensure that all tax obligations and possibilities are correctly taken into account.

Answer: The initiative committee is of the opinion that an import ban on foie gras is compatible with international trade obligations, since all agreements provide for exceptions for measures necessary to protect public morals and the life or health of animals. The Federal Council, on the other hand, doubts the compatibility of such a ban with international obligations, in particular with regard to GATT and the TBT Agreement, as an import ban without prior milder measures (e.g. a declaration requirement) would not be proportionate and would lead to an unjustified trade restriction (p. 13).

The Federal Council assesses the impact of accepting the Stopfleber initiative on international trade as negative. It assumes that an import ban on foie gras and foie gras products without prior milder measures (e.g. a declaration requirement) is not proportionate and leads to an unjustified trade restriction, thereby violating GATT and the TBT Agreement.

In particular, the Federal Council fears that an import ban:

* Violates Switzerland's WTO obligations
* Affects agreements with the EU and may lead to trade disputes
* Complicates negotiations on future agreements
* Leads to new trade barriers that hinder market access for agricultural products

The Federal Council is of the opinion that an import ban would not be staggered appropriately and that milder measures, such as a declaration requirement, should be preferred. It has already initiated regulatory revisions that provide for the declaration of forced feeding of geese or ducks in order to improve consumer information and reduce consumption of foie gras and foie gras products. (p. 12-15)

The Federal Council rejects the initiative without a direct counter-proposal and indirect counter-proposal, in particular because an import ban is not compatible with Switzerland's international obligations and entails the risk of trade disputes (p. 2).

Further reasons are:
- A constitutional amendment is not required to achieve the objectives of the initiative.
- Import bans constitute serious interventions in free trade that fundamentally violate Switzerland's WTO legal obligations as well as the agreements with the EU (p. 16).
- The Federal Council has already initiated regulatory revisions that provide for the declaration of force-feeding of geese or ducks.
- New trade barriers would be created, which would make the current negotiations with the EU more difficult (p. 16).
- Consumers could no longer buy the products domestically and also not import them for private consumption.
- The control of imported products would be difficult, in particular because private imports would also have to be controlled at the border (p. 16).

According to the dispatch, the adoption of the initiative would have the following effects on consumers:

* Foie gras and foie gras products could neither be produced nor imported in Switzerland.
* Consumers could no longer buy these products domestically and would also no longer be allowed to import them for private consumption.
* In view of the lack of equivalent alternatives, an import ban would have the consequence that the consumption of foie gras in Switzerland would be made impossible.
* The effects would particularly affect consumers in Romandy and Ticino, as foie gras is more popular there than in German-speaking Switzerland.

(p. 10)

Answer: In the dispatch, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) as well as the Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT Agreement) are mentioned as international legal provisions that speak against an import ban on stuffed liver and stuffed liver products. Furthermore, agreements with the EU, such as the Free Trade Agreement and the Agriculture Agreement, are also mentioned (p. 12-15).
The popular initiative "Yes to the import ban on foie gras (foie gras initiative)" was submitted on 28 December 2023 (p. 2).
According to the dispatch, 102,478 valid signatures were collected for the popular initiative "Yes to an import ban on foie gras (Foie Gras Initiative)" (p. 3).
Answer: The Federal Council decided on 5 April 2023 to introduce a declaration requirement for stuffed liver and stuffed liver products (p. 2).

According to the dispatch (p. 6), the following European countries, like Switzerland, have banned the Stopfmast: Denmark, Germany, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Poland, Sweden, and the Czech Republic.

The Federal Council rejects the import ban on foie gras because it is not compatible with Switzerland's international obligations and entails the risk of trade disputes. An import ban would be a serious interference in free trade and could violate WTO legal obligations as well as agreements with the EU. The Federal Council prefers milder measures, such as a declaration requirement for foie gras and foie gras products, to improve animal welfare without jeopardizing international trade relations (p. 2).

The Federal Council does not claim that an import ban on foie gras is compatible with international obligations. On the contrary, it argues that such a ban would violate international agreements such as GATT and the TBT Agreement (p. 13). The Federal Council assumes that an import ban without prior milder measures (e.g. a declaration requirement) is not proportionate and leads to an unjustified trade restriction.

It is the initiative committee that argues that an import ban is compatible with international obligations, as all agreements provide for exceptions for measures necessary to protect public morals and the life or health of animals (p. 7). However, the Federal Council does not share this opinion and emphasizes that an import ban would lead to trade disputes, as it violates the principles of free trade and non-discrimination (p. 12-14).

The Federal Council rejects the initiative "Yes to the import ban on foie gras (foie gras initiative)" because an import ban is not compatible with Switzerland's international obligations and entails the risk of trade disputes. It fears that such a ban would violate the rules of the World Trade Organization (WTO) and agreements with the EU, which could lead to trade restrictions and potential sanctions.

In addition, the Federal Council has already initiated a declaration requirement for foie gras and other products, which provides that consumers are informed about the production methods. This is intended to reduce the consumption of foie gras and improve animal welfare without jeopardizing international trade relations.

The Federal Council is also of the opinion that an import ban would not be proportionate, as it would occur at constitutional level, while a change in law or ordinance would be sufficient. It also fears that such a ban could lead to emotional debates and tensions between the language communities of the country, as foie gras is particularly popular in Romandy and Ticino.

Overall, the Federal Council wants to protect animal welfare, but in a way that is compatible with Switzerland's international obligations and trade relations (p. 2-16).

A foie gras import ban could lead to problems with the EU because it contravenes certain provisions in the agreements between Switzerland and the EU. In particular, the free trade agreement between Switzerland and the EU prohibits new quantitative import restrictions or measures of equivalent effect (Article 13). An import ban on foie gras could be viewed as such a restriction. Furthermore, there is an obligation in the agricultural agreement between Switzerland and the EU to liberalize trade in agricultural products and not to take any measures that could jeopardize this (Article 14, paragraph 2). An import ban on foie gras would run counter to this goal. In addition, France declared foie gras a cultural heritage in 2005, which makes it a protected product in the EU and could make an import ban on French foie gras more difficult (p. 14).

The Federal Council considers the deadline of ten years to be too short and too rigid. It argues that compliance with this deadline would be associated with enormous economic and social costs (p. 12-15). In contrast, the existing sustainability measures are more flexible and pragmatic, as they enable a response to ongoing developments (p. 8). The Federal Council is of the opinion that the development of viable and socially acceptable solutions requires time and that the implementation of the initiative would undermine these efforts (p. 3).

The Federal Council sees the following effects on the economy if the Environmental Responsibility Initiative is accepted, compared to existing measures:

1. **Increased costs**: The requirements for the economy and in particular for the primary sector (agriculture and raw material extraction) as well as the associated costs would increase.
2. **Restriction of economic freedom**: The short transition period would make drastic regulatory and incentive measures necessary with regard to the domestic sales market, thereby restricting economic freedom.
3. **Competitive disadvantage**: Companies that produce for both the Swiss and foreign markets and cannot adapt their production according to the sales country may suffer a competitive disadvantage on the foreign market (with less stringent production requirements) due to higher costs.
4. **Higher investments**: Certain factors of production - in particular machines - would have to be modernized much faster than planned (i.e., before the end of the usual useful life), if this were advantageous from a purely ecological point of view.
5. **Financial expenditure**: The implementation of the initiative would be associated with high financial expenditure, particularly for research and development in the areas of agriculture and food industry.
6. **Trade policy risks**: Trade policy and Switzerland's commitments could be negatively affected by the initiative, leading to problems in negotiating trade agreements.

In contrast, the Federal Council considers the existing measures to be better suited to finding sustainable solutions together with the affected stakeholders. The applicable constitutional provisions on sustainability as well as the goals already set by Parliament and the Federal Council and the measures initiated are balanced and do not require any further supplementation in the sense of the initiative (p. 18).

The Federal Council and the initiators have different positions on the implementation of planetary boundaries in the initiative. The initiators demand that Switzerland reduce its environmental impact within 10 years to a level that is within the framework of planetary boundaries. The Federal Council, on the other hand, is of the opinion that this would be too fast and too radical and that such a reduction would cause enormous economic and social costs.

The Federal Council proposes to continue the ongoing legislative and strategic processes in the various policy areas in order to conserve natural resources more strongly. It refers to the applicable constitutional provisions on sustainability and the goals already set and measures initiated by Parliament and the Federal Council.

The initiators, on the other hand, emphasize that Switzerland must drastically reduce its environmental impact in order to comply with planetary boundaries and preserve natural living conditions in the long term. They demand a consistent safeguarding of the renewability of nature and a reduction of environmental impact within 10 years.

Overall, it can be seen that the Federal Council prefers a more pragmatic and flexible approach to implementing planetary boundaries, while the initiators demand a more radical and faster reduction of environmental impact. (p. 3-5, p. 12-15)

The Federal Council cites several reasons for rejecting the Environmental Responsibility Initiative:

1. **Short and rigid deadline**: The initiative demands that the environmental impact caused by consumption in Switzerland be reduced to a level within planetary boundaries within ten years. The Federal Council considers this deadline too short and too rigid.

2. **Enormous transformation costs**: Implementing the initiative would result in enormous transformation costs for the state, economy, and society. These costs would be disproportionate and unbearable.

3. **Negative effects on the economy**: The initiative would lead to a restriction of economic freedoms, which would reduce prosperity in Switzerland. The range of products would decrease, prices of some products would rise, and jobs in Switzerland would be at risk.

4. **Trade policy risks**: The initiative could lead to trade policy risks, particularly if Switzerland introduces unilateral regulations that restrict the import of environmentally damaging products.

5. **Compatibility with international commitments**: The Federal Council has concerns regarding the compatibility of the initiative with Switzerland's international commitments, especially in the area of trade law.

6. **Existing constitutional provisions and laws**: The Federal Council points out that the Federal Constitution already contains numerous provisions on sustainability and that Parliament and the Federal Council have already set various goals and initiated measures to conserve natural resources. Therefore, a further amendment in the sense of the initiative is not necessary.

Overall, the Federal Council considers the initiative too radical and its implementation too expensive and too risky. It therefore recommends rejecting the initiative and instead continuing the ongoing legislative and strategic processes in the various policy areas (p. 2-20).

Answer: The existing constitutional provisions on sustainability play an important role in the dispatch. The Federal Council refers to the fact that the Federal Constitution already contains numerous provisions on sustainability, such as Article 2 paragraphs 2 and 4 of the Federal Constitution, Article 73 of the Federal Constitution, Article 74 of the Federal Constitution, Article 104 paragraph 1 of the Federal Constitution and Article 104a of the Federal Constitution. These provisions require sustainable development, environmental protection and the permanent preservation of natural bases of life. The Federal Council argues that these provisions already provide a sufficient framework for sustainability and that the popular initiative "For a responsible economy within planetary limits" is not necessary (p. 7-9).

The Federal Council sees the following problematic effects on society in the event of the adoption of the initiative:

1. **Strong and rapid adaptations**: The short transition period of ten years would necessitate strong and rapid adaptations in consumption and economy.
2. **Price increases and decreasing range of offers**: This would lead to price increases and a decrease in the range of offers, particularly for environmentally relevant products such as food, housing, mobility, and clothing.
3. **Restriction of freedom of choice**: The freedom of choice of consumers would be restricted.
4. **High social adaptation costs**: There would be high social adaptation costs, particularly information and transaction costs.
5. **Job losses**: Employees would be threatened with job loss due to the structural changes in companies, especially persons for whom it is difficult to rapidly further develop their professional competences.
6. **Reinforcement of social inequalities**: The short transition period could even reinforce social inequalities.

The Federal Council emphasizes that although the initiative aims to benefit future generations and demands a socially acceptable design, the effects on society would be problematic (p. 15-16).
Answer: 105,940 valid signatures were submitted for the popular initiative "For a responsible economy within planetary limits (Environmental Responsibility Initiative)" (p. 2).
The deadline specified in the transitional provision of the initiative for compliance with planetary boundaries is ten years after adoption of the initiative (p. 4).

The transitional provision of the initiative (Art. 197 No. 13 BV) names the following areas as relevant for environmental pollution: climate change, loss of biodiversity, water consumption, land use as well as nitrogen and phosphorus input (p. 4).

Answer: The Climate Protection Act (KlG), which was adopted by the voting population on 18 June 2023, contains various provisions relevant in the present context. Thus, the net zero goal 2050 for greenhouse gas emissions domestically is established (Art. 3 para. 1 KlG). The law stipulates that all companies must have net zero emissions by 2050 at the latest (Art. 5 para. 1 KlG). Furthermore, financial assistance for the promotion of new technologies and processes is provided for (Art. 6 KlG). Finally, the central federal administration must have at least net zero emissions by 2040 (Art. 10 KlG) (p. 9).

The Federal Council wants to reject the initiative because it is of the opinion that the proposed measures would be associated with unjustifiable costs, particularly due to the short implementation period of ten years. It fears that Switzerland would have to take rigorous regulatory and incentive measures that would have far-reaching and negative economic as well as social consequences (p. 3). The Federal Council estimates that the implementation of the initiative would lead to high investments for product developments, price increases, and a declining range of offers (p. 16). It is also of the opinion that the initiative would restrict economic freedom and reduce prosperity in Switzerland (p. 17).

The Federal Council prefers instead a pragmatic and flexible approach that enables the conservation of natural resources without overburdening the economy and society (p. 15). It refers to the already existing constitutional provisions on sustainability and the goals and measures set by it and Parliament to preserve natural resources (p. 8-9). The Federal Council is of the opinion that these approaches are better suited to finding sustainable solutions than the strict requirements of the initiative (p. 18).

Answer: The Federal Council rejects the initiative because it is of the opinion that the demanded deadline of ten years is too short and the implementation of the initiative would be associated with enormous economic and social costs (p. 3). It argues that Switzerland is already on the way to a sustainable use of resources and that the applicable constitutional provisions on sustainability are balanced and do not require any further additions (p. 19). The Federal Council thus prioritizes economic interests and the preservation of Switzerland's competitiveness over social and ecological concerns, by highlighting the potential negative effects of the initiative on the economy and society (p. 15-18).

According to the dispatch (p. 16), there would be price increases and a decline in the variety of offerings for particularly environmentally relevant products, such as in the areas of nutrition, housing, mobility, and clothing, if the initiative is implemented. However, the exact extent of the price increases is not specified. It is merely mentioned that the product selection would become smaller and the prices of some products would rise (p. 18).

Yes, the adoption of the initiative would endanger our jobs in Switzerland. In particular, industries such as agriculture, the food industry, the construction and real estate sector as well as the textile industry would be affected (p. 16). Due to the necessary adjustments and investments in these industries, jobs could be lost, especially in companies that are not able to adapt their production to the new requirements. It is also mentioned that employees would be threatened with job loss due to the structural changes in companies, especially persons for whom it is difficult to rapidly further develop their professional skills (p. 16).
